why_how.text: Michigan only issues an original license to a legal resident, so residency comes before the license application.
Michigan allows one valid license at a time, which is why the old card is invalidated once your application is accepted.

scenario.text: Rosa moves from Texas with her car and her Texas license, and she has not yet established residency.

reasoning.text: Vehicle title and registration are immediate, but the license application waits until residency is established.

result.text: Rosa titles and registers the car right away and keeps driving on her Texas license until she becomes a resident.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the old license stays valid until the new Michigan card shows up in the mail.

correction.text: The out-of-state license is invalidated when the Michigan application is accepted, not when the card arrives.

memory_support.text: Car now, license later, one card only.

prompt.text: A new resident's application was accepted yesterday and the card has not arrived. Is the old license still valid?

answer.text: No. It was invalidated when the application was accepted.

rationale.text: Acceptance of the Michigan application, not delivery of the card, ends the old license because only one license may be valid.

lines.text: Your car and your license follow different clocks.

narration.text: Welcome to the first lesson on moving your driving life to Michigan. Before anything else, the state needs to know you are a resident, and that word has a specific meaning here. Then there are two separate jobs to handle: the paperwork for your vehicle and the license in your wallet. They do not happen on the same schedule, and mixing up their timing is one of the easiest ways to get a practice question wrong. By the end of this lesson you will know who counts as a resident, what to do right away, and what can wait.

lines.text: No residency, no original license or ID.

narration.text: To count as a Michigan resident you need two things together. You must actually live in Michigan, and you must have shown that you are legally present in the state. One without the other is not enough. This matters because state law bars the Secretary of State from issuing an original driver's license or state ID card to anyone who is not a legal Michigan resident. So when a question describes someone who only has a mailing address, or only has a job lined up, ask yourself whether both parts of residency are actually there before answering.

lines.text: Hand in the old title or ownership proof.
Go to a Secretary of State office.

narration.text: Your vehicle is the part with no waiting period. A new resident must title and register their vehicle at a Secretary of State office right away. When you do, you hand in the title or the proof of ownership from the state you came from. Notice the contrast with the license, which is handled on a different clock. Vehicle title and registration are done immediately, while the driver's license application waits until your residency is established. If a question asks what must happen first, the car paperwork is the answer that does not wait for anything else.

lines.text: Use the old license until residency.
Your old driving record follows you.

narration.text: Your license from another state is not useless the day you arrive. You may keep using it until your Michigan residency is established, and after that you apply for the Michigan card at a Secretary of State office. Your history comes along too. Michigan requests your driving record from your former home state, and that record becomes part of your Michigan driving record. If your out-of-state license is suspended or revoked, you must settle the open issues with that former state before Michigan will accept your application. Michigan does not give you a clean slate.

lines.text: Old card is invalidated and handed back.

narration.text: Michigan lets a driver hold only one valid license at a time. That single rule explains what happens to your old card. Once your Michigan application is accepted, the out-of-state license is invalidated and handed back to you. It is not kept as a spare, and it does not stay valid as a backup while you wait. Think of acceptance as the handoff moment. Before it, the old license works while you are establishing residency. After it, only Michigan's license counts, even if the new plastic card is still on its way to your mailbox.

lines.text: Trap: waiting for the new card.
The old license ends at acceptance.

narration.text: Here is the trap that catches many new residents. It feels natural to believe your old license stays good until the new Michigan card arrives in the mail. That is not the rule. The out-of-state license stays usable only until residency is established, and it is invalidated at the moment the Michigan application is accepted, not when the new card arrives. A related mix-up is timing for the car. Title and registration happen immediately, while the license waits for residency. Keep the two clocks separate and the acceptance moment clear, and these questions become easy points.

Here is a quick check: a new resident's Michigan application was accepted yesterday, and the new card has not arrived yet. Is the out-of-state license in their wallet still valid? Work it through with the rule you just learned. Michigan allows only one valid license at a time, and the handoff happens at acceptance. So the answer is no. The old license was invalidated when the application was accepted, and it is handed back. The arrival date of the new card does not change that. If you answered yes, revisit the one-license rule.

lines.text: Live here and show legal presence.

narration.text: Let us wrap up the move. A Michigan resident lives in the state and has shown legal presence, and only legal residents can get an original license or state ID. Your vehicle comes first: title and register it right away, handing in the old title or ownership proof. Your out-of-state license works until residency is established, your old driving record follows you, and any suspension must be settled with the former state first. Once Michigan accepts your application, the old card is invalidated, because you may hold only one valid license. Car now, license later, one card only.

why_how.text: The record check uses a three-year window, so recent convictions decide whether an application can go forward.

scenario.text: Jamal has never held a license anywhere and has two moving-violation convictions from the last three years.

reasoning.text: A never-licensed applicant is refused at two or more moving-violation convictions within three years of the application date.

result.text: Jamal is refused a Michigan license.

claim.text: Myth: someone who has never been licensed has no record to worry about, so convictions do not matter.

correction.text: The refusal rule is aimed exactly at never-licensed applicants, and two or more moving-violation convictions in three years means refusal.

prompt.text: What is the most convictions an applicant's record may carry in the three years before applying?

rationale.text: The general rule allows no more than one conviction within the three years before you apply.

lines.text: Two rules share one three-year window.

narration.text: In this short lesson we look at your driving record before you are even licensed in Michigan. The state checks for convictions in the years right before you apply, and there are two related rules that use the same three-year window. They sound alike, which is exactly why practice questions like to swap them. One rule speaks to people who have never held a license from any state or country. The other speaks to every applicant. By the end you will be able to tell which rule a question is describing and what result it leads to.

The first rule is about someone who has never held a license from any state or country. If that person's record shows two or more moving-violation convictions within three years of the application date, Michigan refuses the license. The key words are never licensed, moving violation, two or more, and three years. It can seem strange that a person without a license has convictions at all, but the rule is written for exactly that situation. When a question describes a first-time applicant with a couple of recent moving violations, the outcome is a refusal, not a warning or a fine.

lines.text: In the three years before applying.

narration.text: The second rule applies to anyone applying for a license. Your driving record may carry no more than one conviction within the three years before you apply. One is the most you can have. That gives you a simple anchor to compare against the first rule. For the general rule, the allowance is one conviction. For the never-licensed rule, the refusal line is two or more moving-violation convictions. Both look back over the same three years. If you can hold the number one and the number two in their right places, you will not be fooled when the numbers are swapped.

lines.text: Trap: mixing up one and two.

narration.text: This is the trap built into this topic. The two conviction rules differ in a way that is easy to blur. A never-licensed applicant is refused at two or more moving-violation convictions in three years, while any applicant may carry at most one conviction in the three years before applying. A tricky question might say the general limit is two, or that never-licensed applicants get extra leeway. Neither is true. Picture it as two strikes refused and one allowed, both counted over the same three-year window. Read every option for the number and for who it applies to.

Here is a quick check: think about the general rule that covers every applicant. Looking at the three years before you apply, what is the most convictions your record may carry? Hold your answer, then compare. The answer is one conviction. No more than one is allowed in that window. If you said two, you borrowed the number from the other rule, the one that refuses a never-licensed applicant at two or more moving-violation convictions. Keeping those two numbers attached to the right applicant is the whole skill in this lesson, and it shows up often in practice.

lines.text: Never licensed: two or more refused.

narration.text: To close, here is the whole picture in a few lines. Someone who has never held a license from any state or country is refused a Michigan license when their record shows two or more moving-violation convictions within three years of applying. Separately, any applicant's record may carry no more than one conviction in the three years before applying. Both rules look back over the same three years, and the difference is the number and who it applies to. Remember the hook: two strikes refused, one allowed. That short phrase will carry you through these questions on test day.

why_how.text: License requirements differ by type, so the job and the vehicle decide which license you need.
The chauffeur's and commercial licenses use different weight lines, so the vehicle rating sorts drivers between them.
Commercial age lines decide where you may drive: from eighteen only inside Michigan, and from twenty-one across state lines.

scenario.text: Ken's job is mainly driving a delivery truck rated twelve thousand pounds GVWR, a single vehicle.

reasoning.text: The chauffeur's line is ten thousand pounds GVWR driven mainly for work, and the single-vehicle commercial line is twenty-six thousand one pounds.

result.text: Ken needs a chauffeur's license, not a commercial driver's license.

claim.text: Common mistake: believing any truck over ten thousand pounds needs a commercial driver's license.

correction.text: Ten thousand pounds GVWR driven mainly for work is the chauffeur's line; a single vehicle needs a commercial license at twenty-six thousand one pounds GVWR.

memory_support.text: Operator basic, chauffeur for work, commercial heavy.

prompt.text: A nineteen-year-old commercial driver is offered a run into Indiana. May they take it?

answer.text: No. Under twenty-one, commercial driving stays inside Michigan.

rationale.text: Drivers aged eighteen to twenty-one may drive commercially only inside Michigan; crossing state lines needs age twenty-one.

lines.text: Weight and age draw the lines.

narration.text: This lesson sorts out the main kinds of driver's licenses in Michigan. Licensing requirements differ by license type, group designator and endorsement, and specialized licenses such as a chauffeur's license or a commercial driver's license may add testing and a background check. Most of you are working toward the basic license, but practice questions often test whether you can tell the types apart. Two kinds of lines do the sorting: how heavy the vehicle is rated, and how old the driver is. Learn those lines and you can place almost any job description in the right license.

lines.text: Operator's license is the basic license.
Chauffeur's: age sixteen and a written test.
Needed when driving is mainly your job.

narration.text: The operator's license is Michigan's basic driver's license, the one most people carry. A chauffeur's license steps up from there. It needs a minimum age of sixteen and a passed written chauffeur's test. You need it when your job is mainly driving a vehicle rated ten thousand pounds GVWR or more, when you carry passengers or property for hire, or when you drive a bus or school bus. The idea to hold onto is that the chauffeur's license is about driving as your work. A heavy vehicle you only use on weekends is a different question from a job behind the wheel.

lines.text: Single vehicle twenty-six thousand one pounds or more.
Sixteen or more people, counting the driver.

narration.text: A commercial driver's license covers the heaviest and highest-risk driving. You need one for a single vehicle rated twenty-six thousand one pounds GVWR or more. You also need one for a combination towing ten thousand one pounds or more when the combined rating is twenty-six thousand one pounds or more. A vehicle built to carry sixteen or more people, counting the driver, needs one too, and so does any load of placarded hazardous materials. Notice how each trigger is a size, a passenger count or a dangerous load. If none of them is met, a commercial license is not the answer.

lines.text: At least eighteen, suspension-free thirty-six months.
Eighteen to twenty-one: inside Michigan only.
Twenty-one to cross lines or haul hazmat.

narration.text: Commercial drivers face age and record rules too. You must be at least eighteen and suspension-free for the thirty-six months before applying. Drivers aged eighteen to twenty-one may drive commercially only inside Michigan. Age twenty-one is needed to cross state lines or to haul placarded hazardous materials. So the same person can be a legal commercial driver on a run from Detroit to Grand Rapids and still not be allowed on a run into Ohio. When a question gives you an age, check two things: whether the trip leaves Michigan, and whether the load is placarded hazardous material.

lines.text: Chauffeur: ten thousand pounds, mainly for work.
Commercial single vehicle: twenty-six thousand one pounds.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because both licenses involve heavier vehicles, people blur their weight lines. The chauffeur's license threshold is a vehicle rated ten thousand pounds GVWR driven mainly for work, while the commercial license threshold for a single vehicle is twenty-six thousand one pounds GVWR. A delivery truck rated twelve thousand pounds that you drive for your job calls for a chauffeur's license, not a commercial one. A similar trap uses age: eighteen allows commercial driving only inside Michigan, while twenty-one is the line for crossing state lines. Match each number to its license before you choose.

Here is a quick check: a nineteen-year-old with a commercial license is offered a delivery run that crosses into Indiana. May they take it? Think about the age lines you just learned. Commercial drivers between eighteen and twenty-one may drive commercially only inside Michigan, and age twenty-one is needed to cross state lines. So the answer is no, not yet. The same driver could take a run that stays inside Michigan. If the load were placarded hazardous material, the answer would also be no until twenty-one, even on an in-state trip. Age and route decide this one.

lines.text: Commercial is for the heaviest loads.

narration.text: Let us pull this together. The operator's license is the basic license. A chauffeur's license needs age sixteen and a written test, and it is required when your job is mainly driving a vehicle rated ten thousand pounds GVWR or more, carrying passengers or property for hire, or driving a bus. A commercial license covers single vehicles of twenty-six thousand one pounds or more, heavy combinations, vehicles for sixteen or more people, and placarded hazardous materials. Commercial drivers must be eighteen, stay in Michigan until twenty-one, and be suspension-free for thirty-six months before applying.

why_how.text: A valid operator's or chauffeur's license already covers mopeds, so only unlicensed riders need a moped license.
Motorcycle credentials are matched to the machine, which is why a three-wheel restriction exists alongside the full endorsement.

scenario.text: Tess is sixteen, unlicensed, and wants to ride a moped to her summer job with her parent's approval.

reasoning.text: An unlicensed teen age fifteen or older with parental approval may apply for a moped license and must take vision, written knowledge and traffic sign tests.

result.text: Tess may apply for a moped license and must pass the vision, knowledge and sign tests.

claim.text: Myth: every moped rider needs a separate moped license.

correction.text: A valid operator's or chauffeur's license already covers riding a moped; only unlicensed riders need the moped license.

memory_support.text: License covers the moped; trikes need three W.

prompt.text: When must an adult take rider education to earn the CY endorsement?

answer.text: After failing the motorcycle skills test twice.

rationale.text: Rider education is optional for most adults but mandatory after a second failed skills test, and always for riders aged sixteen to seventeen.

narration.text: This lesson covers the credentials that sit on top of or beside a regular license: mopeds, motorcycles, and two special endorsements for towing and farm work. Each one answers a simple question. What machine are you riding or pulling, and do you already hold a license? Practice questions often describe a rider and ask what they need, so we will focus on the deciding details. Watch for whether the person is already licensed, how old they are, how many wheels the motorcycle has, and what kind of trailer or farm load is involved.

lines.text: A valid license already covers mopeds.
Suspended or denied means no moped license.
Unlicensed teens fifteen and up may apply.

narration.text: If you hold a valid operator's or chauffeur's license, it already covers riding a moped, so you do not need anything extra. But a suspended, revoked or denied license makes you ineligible for a moped license, so a moped is not a way around a suspension. For people without a license, an unlicensed teen age fifteen or older with a parent's approval may apply for a moped license. That teen must take vision, written knowledge and traffic sign tests. So the deciding question is always whether the rider already holds a valid license.

lines.text: Rider course, or written plus skills test.
Course required at sixteen and seventeen.
Course required after two failed skills tests.

narration.text: To ride a motorcycle you need a CY endorsement. There are two ways to earn it. You can complete a rider education course, or you can pass the written knowledge test plus a motorcycle skills test. For most adults that is a free choice. The course becomes mandatory in two situations: for riders aged sixteen to seventeen, and for adults who fail the skills test twice. So the course is never required just because someone is new to motorcycles. Age and repeated skills test failures are the two triggers that remove the choice.

lines.text: CY three W: three-wheeled motorcycles only.
Double R: fifth wheel plus a second trailer.

narration.text: Some riders only want three-wheeled motorcycles. A CY three W restriction limits a rider to three-wheeled motorcycles, and it is earned through a three-wheeled safety course or the written test plus a three-wheel skills test. Two other endorsements involve towing and hauling. The recreational double R endorsement, which requires a knowledge test, covers a pickup pulling a fifth-wheel recreational trailer with a second trailer hitched behind it. The farmer endorsement lets farm operations move equipment, livestock and produce, and it may call for a general knowledge test and a combination vehicles test.

lines.text: Unlicensed teen: fifteen, parent, three tests.

narration.text: Let us connect the moped rules into one contrast, because questions love to blur it. A licensed driver needs no moped license at all, while an unlicensed teen needs to be at least fifteen, have parental approval, and pass vision, knowledge and sign tests. The same kind of contrast exists for motorcycles. The full CY endorsement covers motorcycles in general, while the CY three W restriction limits the rider to three-wheeled motorcycles only. In both cases, read who the rider is and what they will ride before picking an answer. The details in the question decide it.

lines.text: Trap: course for every new rider.
Required after two failed skills tests.

narration.text: Here is a common trap. Some learners assume every new motorcycle rider must take the rider education course. That is not the rule. Rider education is optional for most adults but mandatory for riders aged sixteen to seventeen and for adults after a second failed motorcycle skills test. Another trap is the three W restriction. It does not expand what you can ride. It narrows the rider to three-wheeled motorcycles only, while the full CY endorsement covers motorcycles in general. When a question gives an adult who failed the skills test once, the course is still a choice.

lines.text: When does the course become mandatory?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: an adult wants the CY endorsement. Under what condition does the rider education course stop being optional and become mandatory for that adult? Think it through. Most adults can choose between the course and the written plus skills tests. The course becomes required for an adult after they fail the motorcycle skills test twice. For riders aged sixteen to seventeen, the course is always required. If you answered that every new adult rider needs it, go back to the endorsement slide, because the choice is the normal starting point for adults.

lines.text: CY for motorcycles, three W for trikes.
Double R and farmer cover special hauling.

narration.text: To finish, here is what to remember. A valid operator's or chauffeur's license already covers mopeds, but a suspended, revoked or denied license blocks a moped license, and an unlicensed teen fifteen or older needs parental approval and three tests. The CY endorsement comes through a rider course or the written and skills tests, and the course is required at sixteen and seventeen and after two failed skills tests. CY three W limits you to three-wheeled motorcycles. The double R endorsement covers a fifth wheel with a second trailer, and the farmer endorsement covers moving equipment, livestock and produce.

why_how.text: REAL ID matters only for domestic flights and certain federal sites, which is why it is optional for people who do neither.
The cost depends on timing: adding REAL ID at renewal costs nothing extra, while other times trigger the duplicate card fee.

scenario.text: Omar holds an enhanced Michigan license with no star and plans a domestic flight next month.

reasoning.text: Enhanced cards are REAL ID compliant even without a star and receive the star at renewal or replacement.

result.text: Omar's enhanced license already meets the REAL ID requirement for his flight.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a card marked Not for Federal Identification is no longer valid for driving.

correction.text: A standard card marked Not for Federal Identification still works for driving and as identification for checks, rentals, age-restricted items and casinos.

memory_support.text: Look for the star; enhanced already counts.

prompt.text: Someone adds REAL ID to their card halfway between renewals. What do they pay?

rationale.text: REAL ID adds no cost at renewal, but asking for it between renewals triggers the duplicate card fee.

narration.text: This lesson is about REAL ID and the enhanced license, two features that change what your card can do beyond driving. Starting May seventh, twenty twenty-five, Michigan residents need a REAL ID-compliant document to board a domestic flight or to enter certain federal facilities, military bases and nuclear power plants. That does not mean everyone needs one, and it does not change what a card can do on the road. We will cover when you need REAL ID, which documents count, how to spot a compliant Michigan card, and what adding it costs.

From May seventh, twenty twenty-five, a REAL ID-compliant document is needed to board a domestic flight or to enter certain federal facilities, military bases and nuclear power plants. REAL ID itself is optional. You may not need it if you neither fly nor plan to enter those federal sites, or if you hold an acceptable alternative such as a valid U.S. passport. Compliant documents include licenses and IDs from states meeting the federal standard and valid U.S. passports and passport cards, and the TSA lists acceptable documents at tsa.gov. So the question is about your travel, not your driving.

lines.text: Or a star inside a Michigan outline.
Enhanced cards comply even without a star.

narration.text: How do you know your Michigan card is REAL ID compliant? Look at the upper right corner. A compliant card shows a star in a gold circle or a star inside a Michigan outline. Enhanced cards are a special case. An enhanced driver's license lets you come back into the United States from Canada, Mexico, Bermuda and the Caribbean, by land or by sea, with no other identity papers, and enhanced cards are also REAL ID compliant. An enhanced card without a star still complies and receives the star at renewal or replacement. So a missing star on an enhanced card is not a problem.

lines.text: Standard card: Not for Federal Identification.
Still valid for driving and ID.
Free at renewal, duplicate fee otherwise.

narration.text: A standard card without REAL ID is marked Not for Federal Identification. It still works for driving and as identification for cashing checks, renting vehicles, buying age-restricted items and entering casinos. What it cannot do is serve as your REAL ID document at the airport or those federal sites. If you decide to add REAL ID, timing affects the price. Adding REAL ID costs nothing extra when you renew, but applying for it at any other time means paying the duplicate card fee. That makes renewal the natural moment to add it if you want it.

lines.text: Standard marked Not for Federal Identification: not compliant.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two cards can look equally plain, but they are not equal for REAL ID. An enhanced card without a star is already REAL ID compliant, while a standard card marked Not for Federal Identification is not, even though both remain valid for driving. Questions might suggest that a card without a star never complies, or that a standard card cannot be used to drive. Both ideas are wrong. A second trap is cost: adding REAL ID at renewal is free, while asking between renewals brings the duplicate card fee. Read the card type and the timing carefully.

Here is a quick check: a driver decides to add REAL ID to their Michigan card about halfway between renewals. What do they pay? Recall the timing rule. Adding REAL ID costs nothing extra when you renew, but asking for it at any other time means paying the duplicate card fee. So this driver pays the duplicate card fee. If they had waited until their renewal, there would have been no extra cost. If you answered that it is always free, look again at the difference between renewal and the time in between, because that is exactly what the question tests.

lines.text: Needed for flights and some federal sites.
Look for the star; enhanced already counts.

narration.text: To wrap up REAL ID, remember the purpose first. From May seventh, twenty twenty-five, you need a compliant document for domestic flights and certain federal sites, but REAL ID is optional if you do neither or hold an alternative like a valid passport. A compliant Michigan card shows a star in a gold circle or inside a Michigan outline, and enhanced cards comply even before they get the star. A standard card marked Not for Federal Identification still works for driving and everyday ID. Adding REAL ID is free at renewal and costs the duplicate card fee at other times.

why_how.text: A license from another state, Canada, Germany or Korea converts without testing, so only some newcomers face the knowledge test, TIP and skills test.
Under-eighteen applicants must go through Graduated Driver Licensing unless they have more than a year of valid out-of-state licensing.

scenario.text: Hana moves from Canada with a valid Canadian license and brings her documents to a Secretary of State office.

reasoning.text: After document approval comes the vision test, and a valid license from Canada converts without the knowledge test, TIP or skills test.

result.text: Hana takes the vision test and converts her license without the other tests.

claim.text: Myth: every newcomer must retake the written knowledge test and the driving skills test.

correction.text: Licenses from another U.S. state, Canada, Germany or the Republic of Korea convert without the knowledge test, TIP or skills test; expired licenses are the ones that need a TIP and skills test.

prompt.text: A newcomer's out-of-state license expired five years ago. What must happen before Michigan issues a license?

answer.text: They must get a TIP and pass a driving skills test.

rationale.text: An out-of-state license expired for at least four years sends you through a TIP and a skills test.

narration.text: This lesson follows a newcomer from the counter to the mailbox. If you moved from another state or country, there is a clear order of steps once your residency is established. You bring documents, take a vision test, and then either convert your license or take more tests, depending on where your license came from and whether it is still valid. At the end there is a photo, a fee and a card in the mail. We will also cover what is different for applicants under eighteen, and the one situation where their extra step is waived.

lines.text: Proof of citizenship or legal presence.
Proof of identity and Michigan residency.

narration.text: Newcomers from another state or country should apply for a Michigan license once residency is established. When you go, bring proof of four things: a Social Security number, U.S. citizenship or legal presence, your identity, and your Michigan residency. Each proof answers a different question, so one document rarely covers everything. Think of the list as number, status, identity and address. A practice question might offer only an old license or only a letter, and that is not enough. The application moves forward once all four kinds of proof are approved, and then testing begins.

lines.text: May also need knowledge test, TIP, skills test.

narration.text: After your documents are approved, a vision test is given. Depending on your situation, a newcomer may also need the written knowledge test, a temporary instruction permit, known as a TIP, and a driving skills test. Notice the word may. Not every newcomer takes all of these, and the next slide explains who skips them. At the end of the process your photo is taken and a fee set by license type and add-ons is charged. Your new Michigan license should then arrive by mail in about three weeks, so it is not printed at the counter.

lines.text: Another state, Canada, Germany, Korea: convert.
Expired foreign license: TIP and skills test.

narration.text: Here is who skips the extra tests. A license from another U.S. state, Canada, Germany or the Republic of Korea can be converted to a Michigan license without the knowledge test, TIP or skills test. Expired licenses are different. Holding an expired foreign license, or an out-of-state license expired for at least four years, means you must get a TIP and pass a driving skills test before Michigan issues a license. So two details decide your path: where the license came from, and whether it is still valid or has been expired for a long time.

lines.text: Graduated licenses come through driver education.
Waived after a year licensed elsewhere.

narration.text: Teens have a separate track. Graduated licenses, namely the Level one Learner's, Level two Intermediate and Level three Full, are issued through Michigan's driver education program for teens under eighteen. Applicants under eighteen must complete Graduated Driver Licensing. That step is waived for anyone who has held a valid license from another state for more than a year. So a seventeen-year-old who moves here after two years of licensed driving in another state does not restart the graduated levels, while a seventeen-year-old with only a few months of licensing still goes through GDL.

lines.text: Valid licenses from listed places convert.
Expired ones mean TIP plus skills.

narration.text: Here is the trap. It is tempting to assume every newcomer retakes everything, or that every license converts. Neither is right. Licenses from another U.S. state, Canada, Germany or South Korea convert without testing, while an expired foreign license or an out-of-state license expired for at least four years sends you through a TIP and a skills test. A second trap is the teen waiver. The Graduated Driver Licensing requirement for under-eighteen applicants is waived only when the teen has held a valid license from another state for more than a year. Check the place, validity and time.

Here is a quick check: a newcomer's out-of-state license expired five years ago. What must happen before Michigan issues them a license? Use the conversion rule. A valid license from another state converts without testing, but an out-of-state license expired for at least four years means getting a TIP and passing a driving skills test. Five years is more than four, so this newcomer must get a TIP and pass the skills test. If you said they simply convert, notice that conversion without testing depends on the license still being valid, which this one is not.

lines.text: Four kinds of proof, then a vision test.

narration.text: To close, here is the newcomer path. Once residency is established, bring proof of a Social Security number, citizenship or legal presence, identity and Michigan residency. After approval you take a vision test, and you may need the knowledge test, a TIP and a skills test. Valid licenses from another state, Canada, Germany or Korea convert without those tests, while expired foreign licenses and out-of-state licenses expired four years or more need a TIP and skills test. Under-eighteen applicants complete GDL unless licensed in another state for over a year. Your card arrives by mail in about three weeks.
